strengths: Addresses well-motivated and practically important problem of concept shift detection and attribution, particularly relevant in healthcare where shifts have clear scientific implications
Strong empirical results: SGShift achieves AUC > 0.9 and recall > 90% across semi-synthetic and real experiments, typically 2-3x better than baselines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 16 model configurations, semi-synthetic ground truth validation, real-world results validated against medical literature (e.g., COVID-19 Omicron findings)
Solid theoretical contributions: Theorem 4.1 provides convergence guarantees for GAM estimation with offset terms, and Lemma 4.2 rigorously extends knockoffs to provide both PFER and FDR control
Interpretability focus: Using GAMs as transparent update terms is valuable, enabling interpretation even when base models are black-box
Good reproducibility: Code available in supplement, detailed preprocessing for each dataset, all hyperparameters specified, multiple public datasets with fetching code for restricted data
Convincing real-world validation: Figure 2 demonstrates that true concept shifts in practice are indeed sparse with characteristic elbow shapes, supporting core assumption
weaknesses: Critical ambiguity about basis function selection: The paper never explains how φ(X) are chosen in practice (splines, polynomials, automated selection?), despite this being central to both theory and implementation, severely limiting reproducibility

Restrictive modeling assumption that concept shift can be represented as linear combinations of fixed basis functions is strong and never validated empirically; authors claim good performance 'even when this assumption falters' but provide no evidence or analysis

Limited methodological novelty: GAMs, L1 regularization, and knockoffs are established techniques; core contribution (adding sparse correction term) is relatively straightforward; Theorem 4.1 is incremental adaptation of standard lasso analysis

Narrow experimental scope: only 3 real datasets, all from healthcare domain; tabular data only; semi-synthetic setup uses additive perturbations potentially favoring an additive shift model; no comparison to SJS [CZZ22] despite similar scope
Missing practical guidance: method identifies shifted features but provides no guidance on downstream use (retraining, reweighting) or demonstration that identified features enable model improvement

Unclear basis function handling for mixed data types: while Model-X knockoffs require i.i.d. features and construction details are non-trivial for categorical variables in healthcare, these challenges are not addressed
Hyperparameter selection not discussed: unclear how λ is chosen (grid search, cross-validation?), and sensitivity to B, π choices for knockoffs is not analyzed
Large confidence intervals in aggregated results (Figure 1) may obscure concerning performance variation; individual model results in appendix show more consistent patterns but receive less emphasis

Strong sparsity assumption without guidance on failure modes: authors acknowledge dense shifts 'may exist and be difficult to explain' but provide no method to detect when shifts are too dense or analysis of graceful degradation

Unclear comparison to baselines: WhyShift is claimed as 'directly comparable' but methods are substantially different (separate model training vs. explicit shift modeling); comparison setup and fair baseline configuration not fully detailed

strengths: Novel and practical problem formulation: Reformulating concept shift diagnosis as learning a sparse correction to a source model elegantly avoids error accumulation of plugin approaches and provides an interpretable framework.

Solid theoretical contributions: Theorems 3.1-3.3 provide estimation consistency and FDR control guarantees, with the key advantage of allowing ET[Y|X] to be nonparametric while only requiring well-specification of the correction form.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 48 semi-synthetic settings across 3 datasets with systematic testing of sparse/dense shifts, varying sample sizes, and complex scenarios (high-dimensional, correlated features, low SNR); consistent 0.1-0.2 AUC improvements over baselines.

Strong real-data validation: COVID-19 case study correctly identifies respiratory failure reduction with Omicron (validated against medical literature); Lupus ancestry study identifies eQTL-backed genes; large-scale ACS validation on 87 cases shows sparsity holds empirically.

Practical and flexible methodology: Three variants (SGShift, SGShift-A, SGShift-K) provide options for prediction correction, feature selection, and FDR-controlled selection; handles source model misspecification through absorption term.

Robustness to assumption violations: Despite assuming sparsity, method maintains strong performance (AUC >0.8) in dense shift settings and with high feature correlation, suggesting practical resilience beyond theory.
Sample efficiency: Demonstrates ability to identify >50% of shifted features with only 100 target-domain samples (SGShift-K in Figure 1), enabling practical online learning applications.
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Theorem 3.1 only guarantees estimation consistency, not exact support recovery. No theoretical explanation for why method performs well in dense shift settings (Table 1) where sparsity assumption is violated, though empirical robustness is demonstrated.

Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is applying L1-regularized GAM to a correction term—a straightforward combination of existing techniques. Knockoff application directly adapts Candès et al. (2018); SGShift-A's hierarchical regularization is pragmatic but not deeply novel.

Incomplete experimental comparisons: Missing comparisons with Singh et al. (2024, 2025), Chen et al. (2022), and Zhang et al. (2023) despite citing these as related work addressing similar problems; limited to 3 baselines (Diff, WhyShift, SHAP).

Methodological parameter choices lack justification: Lambda selection via cross-validation for feature selection (not prediction) may be suboptimal; hierarchical regularization parameter c chosen from range 0.1-0.9 without principled guidance; knockoff aggregation requires specifying B without practical guidance.

Scope limitations: Restricted to tabular data; requires labeled target domain data (unlike unlabeled methods); computational complexity not analyzed; identifies predictive shifts only, not causal mechanisms, limiting scientific interpretability.

Real-data validation scope: Only 3 healthcare datasets limits domain diversity; COVID-19 and Lupus findings validated post-hoc against known biology rather than against ground-truth shifted features; ACS income dataset results mentioned but insufficiently detailed.

Heuristic penalty calibration (Appendix F) relies on orthogonal design assumption that may not hold for correlated features; well-specification assumption in Eq. 1 is strong with violation modes not discussed; degradation under poor source model h_S not analyzed.
